questions.title: How does body-cam video affect the standard of review on consent—clear error or something closer to de novo?
questions.question_body: The panel says it reviews the voluntariness and scope findings for clear error, but then leans heavily on the body-cam footage and cites Scott v. Harris and Norville for the idea that video can "evaporate" factual disputes. If the video clearly captures tone, pauses, and exact wording, does that narrow deference to the district court's findings? In the Seventh Circuit, does video evidence permit the appellate court to independently interpret what happened at the door, or is it still strictly clear-error review of the district court’s inferences from the video?

questions.title: Does telling a resident "we almost need to come inside" make any ensuing "Okay" consent involuntary under Bumper?
questions.question_body: Here the officer said, "I’m sensing that we almost need to come inside to make sure [the kids are okay]," and Lisa replied "Okay" and then facilitated entry. The court treats this as a permissible request, not a claim of authority. Where is the line between a request phrased with urgency ("need to") and an assertion of authority that would render consent involuntary under Bumper v. North Carolina? What factors tip this from coercion to voluntariness—e.g., her earlier refusal, the officer’s tone, or the domestic-violence context?

questions.title: Does Georgia v. Randolph bar third-party consent when the potentially objecting co-occupant is inside but not present at the doorway?
questions.question_body: Lisa consented to entry while her husband (the defendant) was in a back bedroom and unaware of the doorway exchange. Under Randolph, a physically present co-occupant’s objection controls over consent. But Fernandez later limited Randolph. In this scenario, did officers have any obligation to seek or heed Coleman’s views before entering? If he had objected once they were inside, would that retroactively defeat Lisa’s consent to the initial entry or only limit further searching?

questions.title: Did consent to "make sure the kids are okay" authorize a scan for and encounter with the husband in a separate bedroom?
questions.question_body: The court says the officers acted within the scope of consent because ensuring the children’s welfare "necessarily required" scanning the home, locating everyone, and asking basic questions. How do courts define the scope when consent is limited to a welfare check on kids in one room? Is entering other rooms to locate a potentially dangerous adult viewed as within consent (Florida v. Jimeno’s objective reasonableness test) or as a separate protective sweep that would require Buie-type justification?

questions.title: Was the officer’s brief door-crack before consent a Fourth Amendment entry, and if so, is later consent tainted or attenuated?
questions.question_body: Before Lisa returned, the officer "cracked the door and called into the house several times" out of concern. Is cracking the door itself an entry/search triggering the Fourth Amendment? If that step was unlawful, can Lisa’s subsequent consent purge the taint (attenuation), or would the government need to justify that initial intrusion under the emergency aid or exigent-circumstances doctrines?

questions.title: If the initial entry were unlawful, would the later warrant be saved by independent source or inevitable discovery?
questions.question_body: The officers obtained a warrant based on information learned after entering (including the children’s statements about a gun). If the doorway consent failed, could the warrant still stand under Murray/Segura’s independent-source doctrine or Nix’s inevitable discovery? How do courts treat probable cause built on statements/interviews conducted during an unlawful presence—does that taint the warrant unless there’s a separate, untainted basis?

questions.title: How much does failure to advise of the right to refuse matter in domestic-violence consent cases under Schneckloth?
questions.question_body: The court notes the officer didn’t tell Lisa she could refuse, but treats the voluntariness factors as satisfied given her earlier refusal and the officer’s calm demeanor. In assessing consent from a putative DV victim at 4 a.m., how do courts weigh Schneckloth factors like vulnerability, stress, number of officers, and time of night? Is a prior refusal generally strong evidence of voluntariness even without an explicit advisement of the right to refuse?

questions.title: Could emergency aid or exigent circumstances have justified entry without consent after the 911 threat-to-kill report?
questions.question_body: The court declined to reach exigent circumstances and inevitable discovery. Given a 911 report that a husband threatened to kill his wife, the wife’s hesitancy about the kids’ safety, and her temporary disappearance inside, what is the threshold in the Seventh Circuit for the emergency-aid/exigent-circumstances entry into a home? Post-Caniglia v. Strom, is this framed strictly as emergency aid (distinct from community caretaking), and would these facts typically meet it even without consent?
